title: The Sign of the Four
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
setting: London in 1888: Baker Street, a new terrace in south London, a dug-over garden in Upper Norwood and the Thames below the Tower; then, in a prisoner’s story, Agra in 1857 and the convict settlement on the Andaman Islands
lengthNote: Twelve chapters, the last of which is nearly a fifth of the book and belongs to the criminal
openingLine: Sherlock Holmes took his bottle from the corner of the mantel-piece and his hypodermic syringe from its neat morocco case.
summary: A governess who has been sent a pearl every year by a stranger asks Holmes to go with her to meet him. By midnight there is a dead man in a locked room in Norwood, a child-sized footprint in creosote, and an empty place where a chest of Indian jewels stood. Holmes finds the men; he does not recover the treasure, and the explanation is left to the thief, who tells a story of 1857 in which the jewels were never honestly anybody’s. The book runs on a contradiction it does not resolve: it treats the fortune as loot and a curse, and treats the people it was taken from as scenery or as monsters.
referenceStyle: chapter, numbered I to XII as the novel numbers them

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Sign of the Four (eBook 2097)
sourceText.note: A transcription with British spelling and the twelve titled chapters. It prints the title as the magazine did, with the second the; inside the text the phrase appears both as the sign of the four and the sign of four. Its spellings are kept here, including stanch, Hindoo and Mahomet.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: At Southsea, where Doyle was still in practice as a doctor, after an American editor asked him for a story over dinner at the Langham Hotel.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Complete in one issue of Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine; Spencer Blackett’s book followed in October as The Sign of Four.

atAGlance.label: Place in the series
atAGlance.note: After A Study in Scarlet and before the short stories that made Holmes famous. The cocaine, the boredom and Watson’s marriage all start here.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.value: Eleven chapters of pursuit, one of confession
atAGlance.note: Holmes identifies the culprits by the end of chapter VIII. What he cannot supply is the reason, which takes Jonathan Small a whole chapter and thirty years.

structure.label: Chapters I–II
structure.title: A needle, a watch and a client with six pearls
structure.summary: Watson finally protests about the cocaine, and Holmes answers with a lecture on method and a reading of Watson’s dead brother from the scratches on his watch. Mary Morstan arrives with a father missing since 1878, a pearl for every year since 1882, and a letter asking her to be outside the Lyceum at seven. Watson notices the client more than the case.

scenes.title: The Science of Deduction
scenes.summary: The seven-per-cent solution, Holmes’s complaint that Watson has made a romance of his first case, and the watch.

scenes.title: The Statement of the Case
scenes.summary: Mary Morstan’s account: Captain Morstan’s disappearance, the advertisement, the pearls and the anonymous letter.

structure.label: Chapters III–IV
structure.title: Thaddeus Sholto’s story
structure.summary: A cab takes the three of them through fog to a half-built suburb, where a Hindu servant opens the door on Thaddeus Sholto, his hookah and his tiger-skins. He explains that his father, Major Sholto, brought the Agra treasure home, saw Captain Morstan die in an argument over it, hid the body and lived in terror of a man with a wooden leg. His brother Bartholomew has just found the chest.

scenes.title: In Quest of a Solution
scenes.summary: A paper with four names and a plan of a fort, the rendezvous at the Lyceum, and the drive south through streets Holmes names one by one.

scenes.title: The Story of the Bald-Headed Man
scenes.summary: Thaddeus Sholto’s sanctum, the Major’s deathbed, the face at the window, and the chaplet from which the pearls were taken.

structure.label: Chapters V–VII
structure.title: A locked room, a thorn and a dog
structure.summary: At Pondicherry Lodge the garden has been dug to pieces by six years of treasure-hunting, and Bartholomew Sholto sits dead at his table with a fixed grin and a poisoned thorn above his ear. Holmes works out that a one-legged man was hauled up by a small barefooted accomplice who came in through the roof. Athelney Jones arrests the household; Holmes borrows a mongrel called Toby and follows creosote across south London.

scenes.title: The Tragedy of Pondicherry Lodge
scenes.summary: The prize-fighter at the gate, the housekeeper’s fright, the face seen through the keyhole, and the card that reads The sign of the four.

scenes.title: Sherlock Holmes Gives a Demonstration
scenes.summary: The rope, the wooden stump’s marks, the footprint in the garret, and Jones’s confident theory that Thaddeus did it.

scenes.title: The Episode of the Barrel
scenes.summary: Watson takes Mary home and fetches Toby; the trail runs to a timber-yard barrel, then back, and ends at a wharf.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–X
structure.title: The search for the Aurora, and the river chase
structure.summary: The fugitives have hired the steam launch Aurora and vanished. Holmes reads out a gazetteer’s account of the Andaman Islanders to name the accomplice, sends his street boys along both banks, and at last finds the launch himself, disguised as an old sailor, in a repair yard. A police boat runs it down at dusk. The Islander raises a blowpipe and is shot; Small’s wooden leg sinks in the mud of the south bank.

scenes.title: The Baker Street Irregulars
scenes.summary: Mordecai Smith’s wharf, the newspaper report, the dozen street boys, and the gazetteer entry.

scenes.title: A Break in the Chain
scenes.summary: Days of nothing, a chastened Athelney Jones, and an asthmatic old seaman who turns out to be Holmes.

scenes.title: The End of the Islander
scenes.summary: Dinner, Jacobson’s Yard, the pursuit downriver, the two pistol shots and the dart in the woodwork.

structure.label: Chapters XI–XII
structure.title: The empty chest, and Jonathan Small’s story
structure.summary: Watson carries the iron chest to Mary Morstan and forces it open: Small has scattered the jewels along five miles of river. With the fortune gone, Watson can propose. Small then tells his story — the crocodile, the indigo plantation, Agra under siege, the murder of the merchant Achmet, the two officers who cheated the four, and the Islander who got him off the Andamans. Watson gets a wife, Jones the credit, Holmes the bottle.

scenes.title: The Great Agra Treasure
scenes.summary: Small’s first remarks in the cabin, the empty chest in Mrs Forrester’s drawing-room, and Thank God.

scenes.title: The Strange Story of Jonathan Small
scenes.summary: The confession entire, from Pershore to Plumstead Marshes, and the last exchange at Baker Street.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.role: The only unofficial consulting detective, by his own description
characters.summary: This is the book that gives him his vices. He injects cocaine three times a day because there is no case, quotes Goethe and Richter, recommends a freethinking history of religion to Watson, boxes, disguises himself and cooks oysters for a policeman. He solves the who and the how within a night. He also loses the treasure, and the ending is careful to show that success leaves him exactly where the first page found him.
characters.clue: He opens the novel reaching for a morocco case and closes it reaching for the same bottle, having in between named two killers from a footprint and a thorn.

characters.name: Dr John Watson
characters.role: Narrator, army surgeon on half-pay, and the book’s lover
characters.summary: He has a weak leg, a thin bank account and a published account of Holmes’s first case, which Holmes dislikes. He falls for the client at sight and spends the middle of the book hoping the investigation he is helping will fail, since success would make her an heiress and him a fortune-hunter. His judgements of faces — hers, the Islander’s, Small’s — are offered as plain observation and deserve more suspicion than he gives them.
characters.clue: A doctor so distracted on a cab ride that he recommends strychnine in large doses as a sedative, and who says Thank God when half a million pounds turns out to be missing.

relationships.label: falls in love with, and proposes to

characters.name: Mary Morstan
characters.role: Governess, client, and heir to a share of the treasure
characters.summary: Sent home from India as a child and orphaned in effect at seventeen, she has kept her father’s papers in order for ten years and brings Holmes a properly documented case. Holmes calls her a model client. The novel then hands her to the love story: she faints, is taken home, and reappears to be shown an empty box. She is the one person with a claim on the jewels who never expresses a wish for them.
characters.clue: She receives a pearl by post on the same day every year for six years, and is visibly relieved when the rest of the chaplet’s treasure turns out to be at the bottom of the Thames.

characters.name: Thaddeus Sholto
characters.role: The Major’s son, aesthete and hypochondriac
characters.summary: Bald at thirty, twitching, wrapped in astrakhan on a close night, he is drawn as a figure of fun and is the only person in the book who tries to do right by Mary Morstan at a cost to himself. His Corot and his hookah were bought with the same money. Doyle makes the decent heir ridiculous and leaves the reader to notice that he is decent.
characters.clue: He lives behind a shabby suburban front in a room hung with tapestries and tiger-skins, and asks a stranger to listen to his mitral valve before he will tell his story.

characters.name: Bartholomew Sholto
characters.role: The other twin, who finds the treasure and dies beside it
characters.summary: He never speaks. He is described by his brother as a little inclined to their father’s fault, works out by measurement that the house has four feet of unexplained height, and breaks through the ceiling to the chest. A reader first sees him through a keyhole, lit by the moon, wearing his brother’s face set in a grin.
characters.clue: He calculates the height of his own house, finds a sealed garret above his laboratory, and is dead within a day of opening it.

characters.name: Major John Sholto
characters.role: Retired officer of the 34th Bombay Infantry; dead before the story opens
characters.summary: He gambled himself into ruin while guarding convicts on the Andamans, bought the secret of the treasure from one of them, fetched it and kept it all. He then concealed his friend Morstan’s body, withheld the daughter’s share for years, and died of fright at a bearded face against the window. He retires to Norwood with native servants and a house named after a French port in India.
characters.clue: An officer who comes home rich, hires two prize-fighters to guard his gate, and once fires a revolver at a harmless tradesman because the man has a wooden leg.

relationships.label: swears an oath to, and breaks it

characters.name: Jonathan Small
characters.role: Worcestershire farm boy, soldier, overseer, convict, and the narrator of chapter XII
characters.summary: He loses a leg to a crocodile, keeps coolies at work on an indigo plantation, helps murder a merchant for a rajah’s jewels and serves twenty years for it. His one fixed virtue is that he keeps faith with his three Indian partners, which the two English officers do not. His account is vivid, self-serving and the only one there is; nobody else alive was at Agra.
characters.clue: He has his name on a plan beside three others, a wooden stump that sinks in Thames mud, and a grievance against the justice system that he states better than anyone answers it.

characters.name: Tonga
characters.role: An Andaman Islander; Small’s companion and the killer of Bartholomew Sholto
characters.summary: He has no line of speech in the book. He is assembled out of a gazetteer entry, a footprint, Watson’s horror and Small’s patronage, and every one of those sources calls him hideous or a savage. What he actually does is recover from an illness, stay with the man who nursed him, sail an open canoe for ten days, get shown at fairs for pennies, and die in the river. Doyle took the portrait from colonial print and added to its errors; it is the part of the novel that most needs to be read against.
characters.clue: The book first knows him as a naked footprint half the size of a man’s, and last sees him as a pair of eyes in the white swirl of the waters.
traits: described only by his enemies and his keeper

characters.name: Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan and Dost Akbar
characters.role: Small’s three partners in the sign of the four
characters.summary: Two troopers on a fort gate and a foster-brother who lures the merchant in. Small calls them Sikhs, and Doyle has given them names that are mostly Muslim, which says how closely he was looking. They plan the murder, recruit Small at knife-point and then keep their word to him for thirty years, and he to them. At the end they are still in the Andaman convict-barracks, and nobody in London gives them another thought.
characters.clue: Three of the four names on Captain Morstan’s paper; the ones the English officers left out when they took the treasure.

characters.name: Athelney Jones
characters.summary: Stout, wheezing and quick to a theory, he arrests Thaddeus, the housekeeper, the gatekeeper and the Indian butler within an hour and has to release two of them the next day. He is not a fool so much as a man who decides first. By chapter IX he is asking for help, and he takes the official credit for an arrest he would have made at the wrong place.
characters.clue: He announces that facts are better than theories while holding a theory that fits none of the facts in the room.

themes.name: Empire and loot
themes.summary: Every fortune in the book was made in India and none of it honestly. A rajah hedging his bets in 1857, four guards at a gate, two officers with gambling debts: the chest passes by murder and fraud into a villa in Norwood, and the consequences follow it up the Thames. Small’s word for it throughout is loot. The novel lets that word stand, and an Indian partner gets the sharpest line on the subject, yet it never imagines the jewels going back; the only possible ends are an English heiress or the riverbed.
themes.development: Pearls in a cardboard box, then an Eastern room in a suburban terrace, then a garden dug up like a goldfield, and finally the story of Agra, told by a man who went out at eighteen with the Queen’s shilling.

themes.name: Race and the colonial gazetteer
themes.summary: Holmes identifies the second man by reading aloud from a reference book, and what it says about the Andaman Islanders — stunted, hideous, cannibal, untameable — is false in nearly every particular. The novel presents it as the latest authority and then confirms it with Watson’s own eyes on the river. Small’s language about India is of the same kind. None of this is incidental colour: the plot needs a killer nobody will mourn, and it builds one out of the prejudices of its sources.
themes.development: A Hindu servant who looks incongruous in a doorway; a footprint read by racial type; the gazetteer; a face on a launch; and a last chapter that talks of black devils while showing the Indian partners keeping faith and the English officers breaking it.

themes.name: Observation, inference and proof
themes.summary: Holmes’s method is set out as doctrine in the first chapter and tested in a garret in the sixth. It is impressive and it has limits the book is frank about. The watch trick wounds a friend. The trail ends at a barrel of creosote. Days pass with nothing. The launch is found by legwork, and the motive is told, not deduced. Detection here gets the men; it does not get the treasure or the truth about Agra.
themes.development: Monographs on tobacco ash and footprints, a demonstration on a watch, a reconstruction from a rope and a thorn, a false scent, a disguise, and then a long silence while the prisoner talks.

themes.name: Justice, oaths and rightful owners
themes.summary: The four call their mark on Major Sholto’s body an act of justice, and the book does not quite laugh at them. Small murdered for the jewels, but he was then cheated by officers who had sworn an oath to him, and his argument from the dock — who has earned this, if not the men who paid twenty years for it? — goes unanswered by Holmes, Watson or Jones. English law can hang him. It has no view on whose the treasure was.
themes.development: An anonymous letter promises a wronged woman justice in chapter II; a card on a corpse claims it in chapter V; Small shouts the word back at a policeman in chapter XII.

themes.name: Marriage and money
themes.summary: Watson’s romance is governed by arithmetic. A half-pay surgeon may court a governess; he may not court the richest heiress in England without looking like what he fears he is. So the love story can only end well if the detective story ends badly, and it does. The neatness is a little chilling: Mary’s legal inheritance is destroyed by a criminal, and the man who loves her thanks God for it to her face.
themes.development: Attraction at first sight, selfishness at the mention of the sum, hands held in the dark garden at Norwood, and a proposal over an empty iron box.

themes.name: Appetite and habit
themes.summary: The book opens on an addiction and keeps finding others. Holmes needs cocaine when he has no problem to work on and says so without shame. Major Sholto could not bear to part with a single pearl he never used. Small’s craving passes from the jewels to revenge. The case cures nobody: it is only, for Holmes, a better stimulant than the one in the morocco case, and when it is over he returns to the first.
themes.development: Three injections a day on the first page, a miser’s deathbed in chapter IV, a lifetime spent on one hatred in chapter XII, and the long white hand going up to the mantelpiece on the last.

themes.name: London
themes.summary: Doyle maps the case across a city that is growing faster than it can be known. Holmes recites the streets south of the river from inside a cab; the brick terraces are tentacles; Norwood hides an Indian fortune behind a wall topped with glass. The Thames is the way the empire’s goods come in and the way the fugitives mean to get out, and the chase ends on marshland that is barely London at all.
themes.development: Fog in the Strand, a new terrace near the Wandsworth Road, a suburban villa, the wharves opposite Millbank, the Pool, and the mud flats by Plumstead.

techniques.name: The chain of inference
techniques.definition: A conclusion presented as a series of small observations, each of which the reader is invited to check.
techniques.inThisBook: The watch in chapter I is the model: conclusion first, protest from Watson, then the scratches round the keyhole and the pawnbroker’s numbers. The garret in chapter VI repeats it with a rope, a stump-mark and a footprint.

techniques.name: Watson’s retrospective narration
techniques.definition: An account given after the event by a narrator who already knows how it ends.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson writes as Mary’s husband — as she has often told me, he says in the garden scene — so the love plot is never in doubt, and his fear of her fortune is confessed from the safety of knowing it was lost.

techniques.name: Embedded histories
techniques.definition: A second, older story told by a character to explain the present one.
techniques.inThisBook: Three are nested in order of distance: Mary’s ten years, Thaddeus’s account of his father’s death, and Small’s thirty-year narrative, which takes over the last chapter and moves the book from Norwood to Agra.

techniques.name: The material clue
techniques.definition: A physical trace that carries the solution before anybody can read it.
techniques.inThisBook: A small bare footprint in creosote, a thorn, a stone-headed club and a scrap of paper with four names: each is on the page before it is understood, and the creosote is the best clue and also the one that leads to a barrel.

techniques.name: Physiognomy
techniques.definition: Treating physical appearance as evidence of character, in the manner of Victorian physiognomy.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson reads refinement in Mary’s face, resolve in Small’s chin and bestiality in Tonga’s features, all with the same confidence. Holmes does it with handwriting. The habit passes as observation and works as prejudice.

techniques.name: Gothic machinery
techniques.definition: Isolated houses, locked rooms, moonlight, inherited guilt and faces at the window used to produce dread.
techniques.inThisBook: Pondicherry Lodge has a walled garden, a hidden garret, a curse-bearing treasure and a dead man grinning through a keyhole. Doyle then has Holmes measure the room with a tape.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: Characters placed side by side so that each shows up what the other lacks.
techniques.inThisBook: Jones’s instant theory against Holmes’s patience; Watson’s feeling against Holmes’s declared coldness; one twin generous and one grasping; and, in Small’s story, three Indian partners who keep an oath beside two English officers who do not.

techniques.name: Biased witnesses
techniques.definition: Narrators with reasons to shape what they report.
techniques.inThisBook: Small expects to be tried for his life and tells his story to the men who will give evidence. He was forced at knife-point; he never touched Sholto; his heart softened before he tripped the merchant. It may all be so. He even says, maybe you gentlemen think that I am just making out a case for myself.

quotations.text: “It is cocaine,” he said,—“a seven-per-cent. solution. Would you care to try it?”
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Watson has at last asked which it is today, morphine or cocaine.
quotations.analysis: The offer is the shock. Holmes does not hide the habit or defend it; he states the concentration like a chemist and passes the case across as he might a cigar. Doyle, a practising doctor writing in 1889, gives Watson the medical objection and gives Holmes the better lines, and the drug was legal. The scene sets the terms of the book: a mind that treats its own body as apparatus.

quotations.text: “My mind,” he said, “rebels at stagnation. Give me problems, give me work, give me the most abstruse cryptogram or the most intricate analysis, and I am in my own proper atmosphere.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: His answer to Watson’s warning about what the drug will do to him.
quotations.analysis: Give me, three times: the grammar is a craving. Holmes describes work and cocaine as substitutes for one another, which makes crime a kind of supply. The client who knocks a few pages later is welcome for the reason the syringe was, and the last sentence of the novel will confirm that the case was only ever an interval between doses.

quotations.text: Detection is, or ought to be, an exact science, and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes reviewing Watson’s pamphlet on the Jefferson Hope case, which he thinks was spoiled by romance.
quotations.analysis: Is, or ought to be: the correction concedes that it is not yet. Holmes goes on to compare Watson’s book to an elopement worked into a proposition of Euclid, and the novel that follows is exactly that — a love story run through a problem. Doyle lets his detective condemn the form of the book he is in, and then writes it anyway.

quotations.text: Was ever such a dreary, dismal, unprofitable world? See how the yellow fog swirls down the street and drifts across the dun-coloured houses.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: At the window, just before the landlady brings up Mary Morstan’s card.
quotations.analysis: Unprofitable is Hamlet’s word for the uses of this world, and Holmes borrows the pose with it. The fog is doing two jobs. It is the London the case will be conducted in, and it is the inside of his head without a problem: yellow, dun, nothing with an edge. A reader is being shown that the great reasoner’s complaint is closer to melancholy than to logic.

quotations.text: “You really are an automaton,—a calculating-machine!” I cried. “There is something positively inhuman in you at times.”
quotations.speaker: Dr John Watson
quotations.context: Watson has remarked on how attractive the client is; Holmes says he did not observe it.
quotations.analysis: Watson is stung on Mary’s behalf, within minutes of meeting her. Holmes answers that the most winning woman he ever knew was hanged for poisoning three children, so the exchange sets feeling against statistics, and the book will need both: Watson’s attention keeps Mary a person, and Holmes’s keeps her a case. The word inhuman will come back, far less playfully, when Watson looks at Tonga.

quotations.text: In an experience of women which extends over many nations and three separate continents, I have never looked upon a face which gave a clearer promise of a refined and sensitive nature.
quotations.context: Watson’s first description of Mary Morstan as she sits down in Baker Street.
quotations.analysis: The boast is comic and Doyle surely knows it, but the method is serious: Watson reads character straight off a face and treats the reading as a promise. He is right about Mary. He will use the identical procedure on the launch in chapter X and find bestiality, and the novel never suggests that a technique which works on a governess might fail on a stranger from the Andamans.

quotations.text: There was something strangely incongruous in this Oriental figure framed in the commonplace doorway of a third-rate suburban dwelling-house.
quotations.context: A servant in a yellow turban opens Thaddeus Sholto’s front door.
quotations.analysis: Watson finds the man incongruous; the plot says he is nothing of the kind. A suburb like this is where Indian money was spent, and the servant is in the doorway because a major came home rich. The sentence frames him like a picture, which is how the book treats almost every Indian it shows in London: as décor that came back with the furniture.

quotations.text: An oasis of art in the howling desert of South London.
quotations.speaker: Thaddeus Sholto
quotations.context: Thaddeus showing his guests into a room of tapestries, tiger-skins and a hookah.
quotations.analysis: Doyle had dined with Oscar Wilde the evening this novel was commissioned, and Thaddeus is an aesthete drawn for laughs. The joke has a point he cannot see. His oasis is furnished from a murdered man’s jewel-box, and the desert he despises is the ordinary England his father’s money let him withdraw from. Taste, in this room, is what plunder looks like a generation on.

quotations.text: The cursed greed which has been my besetting sin through life has withheld from her the treasure, half at least of which should have been hers.
quotations.speaker: Major John Sholto
quotations.context: The Major’s deathbed confession to his sons, as Thaddeus reports it.
quotations.analysis: Half at least should have been hers — and the rest? The dying man reckons only with the English claim on the jewels, his dead friend’s daughter. The four convicts whose secret he bought with an oath, and the rajah before them, do not enter the account. He adds that he made no use of the treasure; possession was the whole pleasure. It is a miser’s confession and it is also, on a small scale, a colonial one.

quotations.text: Surely it was the place of a loyal friend to rejoice at such news; yet I am ashamed to say that selfishness took me by the soul, and that my heart turned as heavy as lead within me.
quotations.context: Thaddeus has put the value of the treasure at not less than half a million sterling.
quotations.analysis: Watson is honest about a feeling that does him no credit, and that honesty is what keeps him likeable through the book. It also gives the narrator a private stake in the outcome. From here the man telling the story of the hunt for the treasure wants it lost, and the reader should hold that in mind when he reports his relief in chapter XI as if it were simple.

quotations.text: How often have I said to you that when you have eliminated the impossible whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth?
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: In the locked room, asking Watson how the second intruder got in.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted rule in detective fiction, and here it is doing modest work: not the door, not the window, not the chimney, so the hole in the roof. As logic it is sound only if the list of possibilities is complete, and Holmes never shows that it is. What the sentence really supplies is tone. It makes a lucky guess into a law, and ‘how often’ makes Watson, and the reader, the slow pupil.

quotations.text: I could not but think what a terrible criminal he would have made had he turned his energy and sagacity against the law, instead of exerting them in its defence.
quotations.context: Watson watching Holmes go over the floor on his knees with a lens and a tape measure.
quotations.analysis: The sentence before this compares Holmes to a trained blood-hound and gives him beady eyes like a bird’s, so the detective is drawn in animal terms chapters before the Islander is. Watson means a compliment. But the book has already shown a Holmes who works for stimulation, not justice, and the thought that his side of the law is a matter of temperament is left in the reader’s mind.

quotations.text: Facts are better than mere theories, after all.
quotations.speaker: Athelney Jones
quotations.context: Jones coming down from the garret, having found the trap-door Holmes had already shown Watson.
quotations.analysis: He is quoting Holmes’s creed back at him and has it upside down. Jones found one fact and hung a prepared theory on it — the brother did it, for the money — while the footprint, the thorn and the wooden stump are all in the room and fit none of it. Doyle makes the official detective the theorist and the amateur the empiricist, and the joke costs Thaddeus Sholto a night in the cells.

quotations.text: It was soothing to catch even that passing glimpse of a tranquil English home in the midst of the wild, dark business which had absorbed us.
quotations.context: Watson leaving Mary at Mrs Forrester’s door at two in the morning: hall-light, stained glass, barometer, stair-rods.
quotations.analysis: English home on one side, wild and dark on the other: Watson sorts the night into domestic and foreign. The case will not let the division stand. The wild business is an English major’s fraud carried out from an English villa, and the income that built such halls came, often enough, from where the treasure did. The glimpse soothes him because it lets him forget that.

quotations.text: They are naturally hideous, having large, misshapen heads, small, fierce eyes, and distorted features.
quotations.context: Holmes reading aloud from the first volume of a new gazetteer, under Andaman Islands.
quotations.analysis: Holmes, who never guesses, takes this on trust because it is in print. The entry goes on to put the people’s height below four feet and to end every shipwreck with a cannibal feast; none of it is true of the Andamanese, who were not cannibals and did not use blowpipes either. Naturally is the word to watch. It makes a judgement about looks into a fact of nature, and the chapter treats a book of colonial hearsay as the same kind of evidence as a footprint.

quotations.text: An injured lady, half a million in treasure, a black cannibal, and a wooden-legged ruffian. They take the place of the conventional dragon or wicked earl.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Cecil Forrester
quotations.context: Mary’s employer, hearing Watson’s account of the case over tea.
quotations.analysis: Doyle lets a character name the genre. Mrs Forrester hears a list of stock parts, and she is right: a man has been cast as the dragon. The remark is light, and it is the most self-aware line in the book, since it admits that the black cannibal is a role the story needed, not a person it met. Mary’s reply, that she cares nothing for the money, turns down the role written for her as well.

quotations.text: Never have I seen features so deeply marked with all bestiality and cruelty.
quotations.context: The searchlight falls on the second figure on the Aurora’s deck, seconds before the shooting.
quotations.analysis: This is the only look the novel takes at Tonga alive, and it is a verdict. Watson has been told what to expect by the gazetteer and sees it: the paragraph calls him a creature, gives him half animal fury, and has both men draw revolvers at the sight of him before he moves. A doctor who prides himself on reading faces reads this one as not human, and the narrative then shoots him. The sentence should be quoted as evidence about Watson and his sources, not about the Andamanese.

quotations.text: Somewhere in the dark ooze at the bottom of the Thames lie the bones of that strange visitor to our shores.
quotations.context: The police launch sweeps the water with its light and finds no body.
quotations.analysis: After creature and savage, visitor is almost courteous, and our shores makes the death a matter of geography: he was not from here. The present tense is the detail to notice. Watson, writing later, leaves the bones in the river beside the jewels, as though the two foreign things the Thames swallowed that night were of a kind. There is no inquest, and nobody asks whether firing was necessary.

quotations.text: To him it brought murder, to Major Sholto it brought fear and guilt, to me it has meant slavery for life.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small in the launch’s cabin, facing the iron box, before his full story.
quotations.analysis: The cursed Indian jewel was a familiar device by 1890, and a convenient one: a curse puts the harm in the stones, and not in the men who stole them. Small’s own sentence knocks down the superstition. Murder, fear, guilt and penal labour are what theft and the law produce without supernatural help. Note also who is missing from his list of victims: the rajah who owned it, and Tonga, who has just died for it.

quotations.text: Whoever had lost a treasure, I knew that night that I had gained one.
quotations.context: Mary has accepted Watson beside the empty chest.
quotations.analysis: The pun closes the love story and gives away its logic. Mary takes the place of the jewels in Watson’s sentence, something gained as the other thing is lost, and whoever waves off the question of whose loss it was. It was hers, in law. The line is meant as tenderness and largely is, but it also completes a plot in which the woman’s fortune had to be destroyed before the man could speak.

quotations.text: Whose loot is this, if it is not ours? Where is the justice that I should give it up to those who have never earned it?
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Athelney Jones has told him that he has thwarted justice by sinking the jewels.
quotations.analysis: Loot came into English from Hindi, and Small uses it without embarrassment: he does not claim the treasure was clean, only that nobody in the room has a better title. Earned is a grotesque word for murder followed by twenty years in a swamp, yet the challenge stands. The Sholtos’ claim rests on fraud and the Crown’s on conquest. Doyle gives the argument to a convict in handcuffs and lets no one reply.

quotations.text: One month India lay as still and peaceful, to all appearance, as Surrey or Kent; the next there were two hundred thousand black devils let loose, and the country was a perfect hell.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small, an overseer on an indigo plantation near Muttra, describing the outbreak of 1857.
quotations.analysis: This is how the rebellion was told in Britain for a generation: a sleeping county, then fiends, with no cause in between. To all appearance is the phrase that lets daylight in, since a country that only looked like Surrey had reasons of its own. The voice is Small’s, a half-educated soldier’s, and Doyle may be characterising him; but nothing in the novel contradicts him, and his Indian partners are the only Indians it allows a motive.

quotations.text: We only ask you to do that which your countrymen come to this land for. We ask you to be rich.
quotations.speaker: Abdullah Khan
quotations.context: At the fort gate in Agra, with a knife at Small’s throat, proposing the murder of the merchant Achmet.
quotations.analysis: The clearest statement about empire in the book, and Doyle gives it to an Indian conspirator by way of an English convict. It removes any difference between what the four are about to do at a side-gate and what the East India Company did at large: both are people coming to this land to be rich. Small does not dispute it. He asks for three minutes and takes the oath, and the sign of the four is, from that moment, a joint venture.

quotations.text: He was stanch and true, was little Tonga. No man ever had a more faithful mate.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small describing the escape from the Andamans in Tonga’s canoe.
quotations.analysis: Set this beside Watson’s bestiality and cruelty: the only man who knew Tonga calls him faithful, and means it. But the praise is a master’s. Little, mate and, elsewhere, hell-hound, imp and poor Tonga are the words for a dog or a child, and the same speaker beat him with a rope’s end. The book offers two accounts of the Islander, a monster and a pet, and no third in which he might have had reasons of his own.

quotations.text: We earned a living at this time by my exhibiting poor Tonga at fairs and other such places as the black cannibal. He would eat raw meat and dance his war-dance: so we always had a hatful of pennies after a day’s work.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: How the two of them lived in England while Small watched Pondicherry Lodge.
quotations.analysis: Here the novel shows, almost by accident, how its own monster was made. The black cannibal is an act, put on for an English crowd that pays to be frightened, and Small knows it is an act; the raw meat is a turn. Mrs Forrester used the same phrase over tea in chapter IX. Doyle sees the fairground trick clearly enough to describe it and does not notice that the gazetteer, and chapter X, are selling the same show.

quotations.text: But love is an emotional thing, and whatever is emotional is opposed to that true cold reason which I place above all things.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes declining to congratulate Watson on his engagement.
quotations.analysis: He has just praised Mary’s genius for the work, in keeping the Agra plan out of all her father’s papers, so the objection is not to her. It is a creed, and the book has tested it. Cold reason found two men and lost half a million pounds; it took a night and a dog to do what a confession then made unnecessary. Holmes places reason above all things in the same breath as he admits to feeling limp as a rag.

quotations.text: “For me,” said Sherlock Holmes, “there still remains the cocaine-bottle.” And he stretched his long white hand up for it.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: The last lines. Watson has observed that he gets a wife and Jones the credit, and asked what is left for Holmes.
quotations.analysis: The novel ends on the gesture it began with, the long white hand and the bottle on the mantelpiece, so the whole case is enclosed between two doses. It is an oddly bleak finish for an adventure story. Everyone else is paid in the ordinary coin of plots, marriage, promotion, the gallows; the hero’s reward is the return of his boredom. Doyle had not yet decided that Holmes would be a series, and he closes him here as a character study of a man who cannot bear to be unoccupied.

timeline.label: The Indian Rebellion
timeline.detail: Beginning among sepoys of the Bengal army in May and spreading across northern India. Europeans from the surrounding country took refuge in the fort at Agra, as Small does, and an action was fought outside the city early in July.

timeline.label: A penal settlement is founded at Port Blair
timeline.detail: The British opened the convict colony on the Andaman Islands in the aftermath of the rebellion, and many of its first prisoners were men sentenced for their part in it. Small and his three partners are sent there.

timeline.label: Arthur Conan Doyle is born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: He studied medicine at the university there and went into general practice at Southsea in 1882.

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins publishes The Moonstone
timeline.detail: The earlier English novel of an Indian jewel looted in wartime and followed home. Collins sends the stone back; Doyle sends it to the bottom of the river.

timeline.label: A Study in Scarlet appears in Beeton’s Christmas Annual
timeline.detail: Holmes and Watson’s first case, which Holmes criticises in the opening chapter of this one. It made little stir.

timeline.label: Commissioned at a dinner at the Langham Hotel
timeline.detail: On 30 August Joseph Marshall Stoddart, over from Philadelphia for Lippincott’s, entertained Doyle and Oscar Wilde and came away with a promise of a story from each. Doyle wrote his that autumn. Wilde’s was The Picture of Dorian Gray. The Langham is where Captain Morstan vanishes.

timeline.label: Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine prints the novel complete
timeline.detail: In the February number, as The Sign of the Four; or, The Problem of the Sholtos.

timeline.label: Spencer Blackett publishes the first book edition
timeline.detail: In October, under the shorter title The Sign of Four, which many later editions keep.

timeline.label: The Holmes short stories begin in the Strand Magazine
timeline.detail: A Scandal in Bohemia appeared in July. It was the monthly stories, not the two novels, that made Holmes a public figure, and sent readers back to this book.

timeline.label: Maurice Elvey films the novel for Stoll Pictures
timeline.detail: A silent feature with Eille Norwood as Holmes, the last of his long run in the part.

timeline.label: Doyle dies at Crowborough in Sussex
timeline.detail: Knighted in 1902, and by then far better known for Holmes than for the historical novels he valued more.

timeline.label: Arthur Wontner plays Holmes in a sound film of the story
timeline.detail: Directed by Graham Cutts, with Ian Hunter as Watson; the plot is rearranged so that the Agra backstory comes first.

timeline.label: Granada Television’s feature-length adaptation
timeline.detail: Jeremy Brett as Holmes and Edward Hardwicke as Watson, directed by Peter Hammond. It drops Watson’s engagement altogether.

places.name: Baker Street, London
places.note: The sitting-room where the novel begins and ends, with the bottle on the corner of the mantelpiece.

places.name: Lyceum Theatre, Strand
places.note: The third pillar from the left, where Mary Morstan is told to wait at seven, and where a coachman collects the three of them in the fog.

places.name: Upper Norwood
places.note: Pondicherry Lodge: Major Sholto’s walled villa, its grounds dug over for six years in search of the chest that was in the roof.

places.name: Langham Hotel, Portland Place
places.note: Captain Morstan’s address on the night he disappeared in 1878, and the hotel where the novel was commissioned over dinner.

places.name: Plumstead Marshes
places.note: The melancholy south bank where the Aurora runs aground, Small’s wooden leg sinks in the mud, and the treasure and the Islander are both lost to the river.

places.name: Agra Fort
places.note: The Mughal fortress on the Yamuna where Small guards a side door in 1857, the merchant Achmet is murdered, and the jewels are first hidden in a wall.

places.name: Port Blair, Andaman Islands
places.note: The convict settlement in the Bay of Bengal where Small serves his sentence, the two officers play cards, and Tonga is found sick in the woods.

places.name: Southsea, Portsmouth
places.note: Where Doyle was in practice as a doctor when he wrote the book, some distance from the London it maps so confidently.

criticalViews.position: An imperial Gothic: the colony comes back to haunt the suburb
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the detective plot is a way of managing a fear. Wealth taken in India comes back to England bringing violence with it, the suburban villa turns out to rest on a crime at Agra, and Holmes’s task is to find the foreign element and remove it. The Thames chase restores a border; the ending tidies the empire’s consequences out of sight.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the book more knowing than it is. Doyle’s sympathies are mixed, not critical: he lets Small call the jewels loot and lets an Indian name the motive of conquest, but he also prints the gazetteer as fact and has his heroes shoot first. A novel can expose a guilty conscience without having one.

criticalViews.position: A racist text that should be taught as one
criticalViews.summary: The portrait of Tonga is drawn from colonial ethnography at its worst, given Holmes’s authority and confirmed by a narrator the reader trusts. He is denied speech, called a creature, and killed without regret. On this view the honest way to read the novel is to say so plainly and to set the gazetteer beside what is actually known of the Andamanese.
criticalViews.counter: The objection is that it can stop too soon. The book contains materials that work against its own caricature — Small’s testimony to Tonga’s loyalty, the fairground act, the faith kept by the Indian partners and broken by the officers — and a reading that only condemns will miss how the prejudice is put together.

criticalViews.summary: The traditional account: this is the novel that codifies Holmes. The watch, the monographs, the rule about the impossible and the reconstruction in the garret establish detection as applied reasoning, and the bungling of Athelney Jones shows what it replaces.
criticalViews.counter: Count the results. The trail ends at a barrel, the launch is found by visiting sixteen boatyards, the treasure is lost and the motive is supplied by confession. Holmes’s one recourse to printed authority is the gazetteer, which is worthless. The method is a performance of certainty as much as a means to it, and the framing scenes with the syringe suggest Doyle knew that.

essayQuestions.question: How does Doyle present the Agra treasure, and what does the novel finally do with it?
plan: Trace the chest’s owners in order — rajah, merchant, the four, Major Sholto, Bartholomew, Small — and note that every transfer is a crime.
Use Abdullah Khan’s we ask you to be rich to show the novel comparing private murder with the business of empire.
Set Major Sholto’s half at least should have been hers against Small’s whose loot is this, and ask whose claims each man leaves out.
Consider the curse as a device that shifts blame from people to stones, and how Small’s own list knocks it down.
Weigh the ending: the jewels cannot go to an English heiress without taint and the book cannot picture them returning to India, so they go into the river.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of Tonga. How far does the novel invite a reader to question it?
plan: Begin with how he is assembled before he appears: a footprint typed by race, then the gazetteer read aloud by Holmes.
Analyse Watson’s description in chapter X — creature, bestiality, half animal fury — and the fact that both men draw before he moves.
Bring in Small’s account: nursed back to health, stanch and true, beaten with a rope’s end, exhibited at fairs as the black cannibal.
Note what the book never gives him: a word of speech, a motive, a burial, an inquest.
Conclude on the limits of the invitation: the materials for doubt are present, but no character voices it and the narrator’s view is never corrected.

essayQuestions.question: Is The Sign of the Four a celebration of reason?
essayQuestions.focus: Holmes’s method, its successes and its failures
plan: Set out the doctrine of chapter I: exact science, never guessing, the monographs, the watch.
Show the method at its best in the garret, with the rope, the stump and the rule about eliminating the impossible.
List what goes wrong: the creosote barrel, the vanished launch, the blank days of chapter IX, the empty chest.
Contrast Holmes with Athelney Jones, and then with Watson, whose feeling the final chapter will not rank below cold reason.
End with the frame: a reasoner who needs cocaine when reason has nothing to work on.

essayQuestions.question: What part does Watson’s love story play in the novel?
plan: Start with Holmes’s complaint that Watson worked a love-story into Euclid, and observe that Doyle proceeds to do so.
Follow the golden barrier from Watson’s selfishness in the cab to Thank God over the box.
Ask what Mary Morstan is allowed to do: a model client in chapter II, largely a prize by chapter XI.
Consider what a narrator who wants the treasure lost does to a reader’s trust in his account.
Compare the three rewards in the last lines — a wife, the credit, the bottle — and what the book thinks each is worth.

discussionQuestions: Holmes and Watson fire at Tonga together, and nobody in the book asks afterwards whether they had to. Should a reader?
Small says the treasure belongs to the four because they earned it. Who, if anyone, has a better claim?
Thaddeus Sholto is made ridiculous and behaves better than anyone else. Why might Doyle have combined those two things?
Watson thanks God that Mary has lost a fortune. Is that love, or self-interest, or both?
The gazetteer is wrong about the Andaman Islanders and Holmes believes it. What does that do to his authority in the rest of the book?
The novel begins and ends with the cocaine bottle. Does the case change Holmes at all?

related.why: The book this one is answering: an Indian jewel seized in a siege, a curse that follows it to an English house, and a very different decision about where it should end up.
The twelve stories that came next and made Holmes famous, with the method intact and Watson now married to the client of this case.
Commissioned at the same dinner by the same editor, and another London book in which a beautiful room is paid for by something kept out of sight upstairs.
Four years earlier: the same fog, the same professional men, and a respectable household with a small, violent figure coming and going by the back way.
Another English fortune with a colonial source and another character from overseas whom the narrator describes as barely human; the comparison sharpens both.
